issues.legal_issue: An amendment to objections against an arbitral award cannot introduce a new ground of misconduct after the original objections have omitted its material facts.
material_facts: An objector filed objections to the award within the applicable period and alleged several acts of misconduct, but did not allege that the arbitrator falsely recorded the objector’s attendance or improperly returned specified documents.

After the arbitrator had died, an amendment sought to add those distinct allegations; the court allowed it, and the High Court treated the new allegations as further particulars of the original objections.
issues.conclusion: The amendments adding the distinct allegations of falsely recording attendance and returning documents were not merely particulars of the original objections and should not have been allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rules 2 and 4 CPC distinguish material facts, which establish the ground of a claim, from particulars, which provide detail about a ground already pleaded. Particulars cannot introduce a new ground of misconduct. The Court relied on Samant N. Balkrishna v. George Fernandez and, by analogy concerning substitution of one pleaded fraud for another, Abdool Hoosein Zenail Abadin v. Charles Agnew Turner.

predicates.arbitration_award_objection: A party filed objections seeking to challenge an arbitral award.
predicates.amendment_adds_new_misconduct_ground: The party later sought to add a distinct allegation of misconduct by the arbitrator.
predicates.original_objection_lacks_that_material_f: The original objections did not state the material facts of that distinct allegation.

issues.definition: When objections to an arbitral award omit the material facts of a misconduct ground, a later amendment adding that ground is not permitted merely as a statement of particulars.

issues.legal_issue: A party is not estopped from challenging an order allowing an amendment merely because costs were awarded when payment of costs was not a condition of allowing the amendment.
material_facts: The amendment order allowed the proposed amendments after considering their merits and separately awarded costs in the court’s discretion.
The amendment order was not conditional on payment of costs, and the challenging parties did not accept that order as a basis for abandoning their challenge.
issues.conclusion: The discretionary award of costs did not estop the parties from challenging the amendment order.
issues.legal_principle: Estoppel from accepting costs applies where the order is conditional and payment of costs is a condition precedent to the relief granted. It does not apply where costs are awarded independently in the exercise of the court’s discretion. The Court discussed Metal Press Works Ltd. v. Guntur Merchants Cotton Press Co. Ltd., Sree Mahant Prayag Dossjee Varu v. Raja Venkata Perumal, Ramcharan Mahto v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Kapura Kuer v. Narain Singh, and J. Devaiah v. Nagappa.

predicates.challenge_to_amendment_order: A party challenged an order allowing an amendment to pleadings.
predicates.costs_awarded_separately: The court awarded costs independently in the exercise of its discretion.
predicates.costs_not_condition_of_relief: Payment of costs was not a condition precedent to allowing the amendment.

issues.definition: A challenge to an amendment order is not barred by estoppel when the costs were awarded separately and were not a condition of the relief.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitral award is not properly set aside for misconduct based on an unsupported, belated allegation about attendance or the return of documents not shown to have been evidence.
material_facts: The allegation that the arbitrator falsely recorded a party’s attendance was first raised after the arbitrator’s death and was not included in the timely original objections.
The allegation was unsupported by corroborating contemporaneous evidence; the party had not raised it before the arbitrator, and the other parties had signed records recording the attendance.
Some municipal assessment statements were taken away for typing and were not produced again, and the record did not show that they had been accepted as evidence or relied on.
The nature of other returned documents was not established, and there was no evidence that they formed part of the evidence produced before the arbitrator.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in finding misconduct on either basis or in setting aside the award on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 30(a) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an award may be set aside for misconduct of the arbitrator or proceedings, but a serious allegation must be supported by reliable evidence. The Court found an uncorroborated assertion, raised belatedly and not tested in cross-examination, insufficient in the circumstances; returning documents was not misconduct where they were not shown to be evidence produced before the arbitrator.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and ((attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_late and attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_uncorroborated) or (documents_were_returned and documents_not_shown_to_be_evidence))

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award on the ground of misconduct.
predicates.attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_late: The allegation that the arbitrator falsely recorded attendance was raised only after the arbitrator had died.
predicates.attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_unco: No corroborating contemporaneous evidence supported the allegation, and it had not been raised before the arbitrator.
predicates.documents_were_returned: The arbitrator returned documents to a party after they had been submitted during the proceedings.
predicates.documents_not_shown_to_be_evidence: The record did not establish that the returned documents formed part of the evidence produced before the arbitrator.

issues.definition: In a challenge to an arbitral award, a belated and uncorroborated attendance allegation, or the return of documents not shown to be evidence, does not establish misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot find an error apparent in an arbitral award by inferring the arbitrator’s reasoning or by relying on valuation evidence that was not presented to the arbitrator.
material_facts: The award stated the market values of the properties but did not disclose the arbitrator’s reasoning for arriving at those values.

A valuation statement covering the immovable properties bore the signatures of all parties, and no party produced other valuation evidence before the arbitrator or objected to the stated valuations during the arbitration.
Additional municipal assessment documents were produced in court but had not been produced before the arbitrator.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in examining the valuation as though the award disclosed a reasoned method and in relying on additional valuation evidence; the valuation objection did not establish an error on the face of the award.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 30(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an error on the face of an award may justify setting it aside where the award or an incorporated document states reasons based on an erroneous legal proposition. A court may not infer reasons from a non-speaking award, probe the arbitrator’s mental process, reassess the evidence, or use evidence not presented to the arbitrator to attack the award. The Court relied on Champsey Bhara and Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spg. and Wvg. Co. Ltd., Jivarajbhai Ujamshi Sheth v. Chintamanrao Balaji, Sudarsan Trading Co. v. Government of Kerala, Raipur Development Authority v. Chokhamal Contractors, and Santa Sila Devi v. Dhirendra Nath Sen.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award in court.
predicates.award_is_non_speaking: The award states the result but does not set out the arbitrator’s reasoning for it.
predicates.valuation_error_requires_inferred_reason: The alleged valuation error can be found only by inferring the arbitrator’s reasoning from the award or the record.
predicates.valuation_challenge_uses_evidence_not_be: The valuation challenge relies on evidence that was not presented to the arbitrator.

issues.definition: A court cannot establish a valuation error on the face of an arbitral award when doing so requires inferring undisclosed reasons or relying on evidence not presented to the arbitrator.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitral award is not invalid because it does not separately list every movable asset or state each party’s advance when it disposes of the claims through a consolidated allocation and provides for later-discovered property.
material_facts: The arbitrator stated that the parties’ claims, accounts, and evidence had been considered.
The award provided that property later recovered, traced, or found available for partition would be divided equally among the parties.
The arbitration agreement required advances to be adjusted against shares, and the proceedings showed that the arbitrator considered the advances before fixing each party’s overall share.
The arbitrator gave consolidated shares rather than separately stating each advance or formally listing a decision on every disputed item.
issues.conclusion: The award could not be set aside for omitting separate decisions on every movable item or for failing to state each advance and its adjustment separately.
issues.legal_principle: Unless the agreement specifically requires a formal decision on each matter, an award is presumed to dispose finally of all matters in difference. A consolidated award is permissible. The Court relied on Santa Sila Devi v. Dhirendra Nath Sen.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and award_provides_for_later_found_property and arbitrator_considered_advances and award_makes_consolidated_allocations

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award for allegedly omitting items or adjustments.
predicates.award_provides_for_later_found_property: The award provides for the division of property later recovered, traced, or found available for partition.
predicates.arbitrator_considered_advances: The proceedings show that the arbitrator considered the parties’ advances before fixing their shares.
predicates.award_makes_consolidated_allocations: The arbitrator allocated overall shares without separately stating every item or adjustment.

issues.definition: An award that provides for later-found property and makes consolidated allocations is not invalid merely because it does not itemize every decision or advance, if the arbitrator considered the advances.

issues.legal_issue: Assigning responsibility for maintaining a family deity to the party receiving the property in which the deity is kept does not invalidate a partition award when the right to worship remains available to all parties.
material_facts: The property containing the family deity and temple was allotted to one party, and responsibility for maintaining the deity was assigned to that party.
The right to worship the deity remained available to all parties.
issues.conclusion: The award was not invalid because it entrusted maintenance of the family deity to the party receiving the property where the deity was kept.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found it proper to entrust maintenance of the deity to the party allotted the property in which the deity was kept, particularly where the right of worship remained available to all parties.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and deity_property_allotted_to_one_party and deity_maintenance_assigned_to_that_party and worship_right_remains_shared

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral partition award.
predicates.deity_property_allotted_to_one_party: The property in which a family deity is kept was allotted to one party.
predicates.deity_maintenance_assigned_to_that_party: That party was assigned responsibility for maintaining the deity.
predicates.worship_right_remains_shared: The other parties retained the right to worship the deity.

issues.definition: An award is not invalid for assigning deity maintenance to the recipient of the deity’s property when all parties retain the right to worship.

issues.legal_issue: The parties’ implementation of an arbitral award by transferring properties allotted under it is an additional circumstance supporting maintenance of the award.
material_facts: During the court proceedings, parties on both sides transferred or agreed to transfer properties allotted to them under the award.
Some transfers asserted ownership on the basis of the award.
issues.conclusion: The parties’ conduct in acting on the award was an additional circumstance supporting its maintenance rather than its being set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the parties’ substantial implementation of the award, including transfers made in reliance on the allotted shares, as an additional circumstance supporting the decision to maintain the award.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award in court.
predicates.parties_transferred_property_under_award: Parties transferred or agreed to transfer property allotted to them under the award while the proceedings were pending.
predicates.transfers_asserted_award_based_ownership: At least some transfers claimed ownership by relying on the award.

issues.definition: When parties to a challenge have transferred allotted property in reliance on an award, their implementation of it is an additional reason to maintain it.
